title: Thermal energy transfers
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: B.1#c22 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c35 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; B.1#c30 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.1#c32 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Specific latent heat L
items.clue: The energy required to change the phase of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature.

items.label: Stefan–Boltzmann law
items.clue: Luminosity is proportional to surface area and to the fourth power of kelvin temperature.

items.label: Convection
items.clue: Transfer of thermal energy in a fluid (liquid or gas) by bulk movement of the fluid itself.

items.label: Thermal radiation
items.clue: Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves emitted from the surface of a body because of its temperature.

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.explanation: P: ΔT = 30 − 10 = 20 °C, which is 20 K because the kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size. Q: ΔT = 310 − 290 = 20 K. The changes are equal.

questions.stem: The average kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is 8.28 × 10⁻²¹ J. Take k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. What is the temperature of the gas in degrees Celsius?
Which of the following is the internal energy of a system?

options.text: The total random kinetic energy of its molecules plus their total intermolecular potential energy
The total random kinetic energy of its molecules, which is the quantity its temperature measures
The kinetic energy of the body's motion plus its gravitational potential energy and its molecules' energy
The quantity of heat that is stored in the system, which it gives out again when it cools down

questions.explanation: This is the guide's definition: the potential energy arising from the forces between molecules plus the kinetic energy of their random motion.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?

options.text: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.

questions.explanation: The direction of the resultant transfer is set by temperature difference alone: from the hotter block to the cooler water. It stops at thermal equilibrium, when the temperatures are equal, just above 20 °C here because the tank is so large.

questions.stem: The specific heat capacity of copper is 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. A student heats a copper block from 15 °C to 65 °C and, before using Q = mcΔT, adds 273 to the temperature change 'because c is given per kelvin'. Which evaluation of the student's method is correct?

options.text: It is correct: every Celsius quantity, including a temperature change, must have 273 added to it before it is used in a physics equation.
It is wrong: a temperature change has the same numerical value in kelvin as in degrees Celsius, since the two scales differ only in where their zero lies.
It is wrong only in the number used: the kelvin and the degree Celsius are different sizes, so ΔT should be multiplied by a factor rather than have 273 added.
It is wrong: the kelvin is simply the SI name for the degree Celsius, so a temperature and a temperature change are both identical on the two scales.

questions.stem: A block of ice at 0 °C melts completely to give water at 0 °C. What happens to the internal energy of the H₂O, and why?

options.text: It is unchanged: the temperature is still 0 °C, and internal energy depends on temperature alone.
It is unchanged: the energy that is absorbed is balanced by the energy released as bonds break.
It increases: intermolecular potential energy rises; the average kinetic energy is unchanged.
It increases: the molecules move faster in the liquid than in the solid at the same temperature.

questions.explanation: The latent heat absorbed breaks the ordered structure of the ice, increasing the intermolecular potential energy. The temperature is constant, so the average random kinetic energy is unchanged; the internal energy (KE + PE) increases by mL_f.

questions.stem: A metal sphere at 33 °C hangs from a thin thread inside a large evacuated chamber whose walls are at 18 °C. Energy is exchanged between the sphere and the walls only by thermal radiation. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?

options.text: Only the sphere emits thermal radiation, since the walls are too cool to radiate, so the whole transfer is from the sphere to the walls.
Both emit thermal radiation, but the sphere emits more than it absorbs, so the resultant transfer is from the sphere to the walls.
The walls contain far more internal energy than the sphere does, so the resultant transfer of energy is from the walls to the sphere.
Coldness radiates from the cool walls towards the sphere, so the resultant transfer is from the walls to the sphere.
